children: Corn for December delivery fell 1.5% to $5.28 3/4 a bushel on the Chicago Board of Trade Wednesday, with traders staying cautious ahead of the Trump-Xi summit in Washington.
Wheat for December delivery fell 1.4% to $7.07 1/4 a bushel.
Soybeans for November fell 0.6% to $13.17 1/2 a bushel.

All Hands on Deck: Many traders were seen today as being risk-off ahead of the summit between President Trump and Chinese leader Xi. While not much is expected in the way of fresh deals guaranteeing Chinese purchases of U.S. agricultural exports, caution remains the overarching sentiment. "Headline risk is pertinent," AgMarket.net said in a note.

Good Vibes Only: While many traders spent the day attempting to factor in the risk potential for headlines out of the Trump-Xi summit, some think that the meeting may produce news that will be supportive for higher prices. "Trump has been playing nice with Asian leaders as of late, even posting a series of pics with Kim Jong Un and Xi in the past couple months," Futures International's Jason Snow said. "So I'd expect more friendly postings once again."

Currency Crunch: The stronger U.S. dollar is another pressure point for grain futures today, Argus said in a note. According to the firm, what's put a lid on corn, soybeans, and wheat futures in recent sessions is how the dollar and Treasury yields have behaved. Grains are now backing up to technical levels that could mean further declines ahead, Argus said. A stronger dollar typically means that U.S. grain exports are less competitive on the world market versus exports from other nations.

Harvest Implications: A potential plan to implement restrictions on diesel exports may have implications for farmers harvesting crops. Energy Secretary Chris Wright hinted at a voluntary cap, rather than a ban, in an interview with The Wall Street Journal. The plan could make diesel cheaper for farmers in the Midwest and Gulf Coast, said Jim Wiesemeyer of Ag Bull, citing research from the Atlantic Council. "Farmers buying fuel during that period could benefit, although savings would depend on local delivery prices and purchase timing," Wiesemeyer said, adding that a ban might lead to refineries lowering their throughput and could actually cause an increase in prices.

Slow Pace: Winter grains are being planted in Russia at the slowest rate in more than a decade, SovEcon said in a note. The firm said that Russian farmers have planted 6.1 million hectares of winter grains as of the end of last week, which is down from 7.1 million hectares at this time last year. The slowdown is a result of "severe financial pressure amid disrupted Black Sea exports," SovEcon said. The last time planting was this slow was in 2013, when an unusually wet season interrupted the planting campaign, the firm said.

Plummeting Production: Average daily ethanol production in the U.S. fell to its lowest level since early May last week, according to data from the EIA. The agency said that average daily production for the week ended Sept. 18 was 1.028 million barrels a day. That's the lowest rate of production since the week ended May 1, when average production was reported at 1.017 million barrels a day. Total ethanol inventories for the week landed at 24.68 million barrels--a reduction of 537,000 barrels from the prior week. Both inventories and average production landed on the low side of forecasts from analysts surveyed by Dow Jones.
The USDA will release its weekly export sales report at 8:30 a.m. ET Thursday.
The USDA will release its quarterly Hogs and Pigs report at 3 p.m. ET Thursday.
The USDA will release its monthly Cold Storage report at 3 p.m. ET Friday.
The CFTC will release its weekly Commitment of Traders report at 3:30 p.m. ET Friday.
